active_themes.label: Warsh Takes the Chair
active_themes.summary: Kevin Warsh confirmed May 14 by 67–32 margin. The market interpretation (Warsh will prioritize financial conditions over inflation) is now locked in. Powell's exit today is ceremonial—the real pivot happened three weeks ago. The open question shifts from 'will the Fed cut' to 'will cuts into $90+ oil push the dollar lower and oil higher, creating a second wave of inflation that forces policy reversal.' Today's 30-year Treasury yield spike (highest since June 2007) suggests bond markets are already pricing that reversal scenario.

active_themes.label: Oil Stays Sticky Above $90
active_themes.summary: No new Iran escalation today, but oil remains the binding constraint on the entire rate-cut narrative. Warsh's confirmation removes the last institutional barrier to cuts, which normally would weaken the dollar and push oil higher. The critical path is now: (1) Warsh signals rate cuts as inflation normalizes, (2) dollar weakens, (3) oil tests $95–100, (4) bond markets reprice inflation expectations upward, (5) yields spike. Today's Treasury move is the market front-running step (5). Oil closed unchanged today, but the 30-year yield move signals the market is now pricing the entire sequence.

active_themes.label: Credit Withdrawal Accelerating
active_themes.summary: Warsh's confirmation accelerates the lender front-running process. Banks and credit card issuers now have the clearest possible signal: the Fed will cut rates despite inflation because Warsh prioritizes financial conditions. Rational lenders will withdraw credit now (before competition for lower-yield lending intensifies) and price deposits for a lower-rate future. Equities rallied into the confirmation on this logic, but today's sell-off reveals the hidden cost: if lenders are pulling credit while oil remains sticky, consumer spending will weaken even as the Fed cuts. That's a configuration that typically leads to capitulation selling once the data arrives.

active_themes.label: Second Lender Move Confirms Pattern
active_themes.summary: No new lender announcement today, but the stage is set for accelerated credit withdrawal over the next 7–14 days. April household debt hit $18.8T all-time high. Lenders know this, know Warsh is confirmed, and now have incentive to front-run the credit cycle. The May 29 consumer spending print will determine whether lenders' pessimism is prophetic (spending weakens, credit was removed at the right time) or premature (spending holds, credit withdrawal was early and creates a self-fulfilling demand destruction). Today's equity sell-off despite hawkish Fed confirmation suggests bond markets are already confident in the pessimistic case.

active_themes.label: Long Yields Hit 2007 Highs
active_themes.summary: 30-year Treasury yields are at their highest since June 2007. This is the single most important signal today and receives no headline coverage. It means bond markets are pricing either structural inflation or currency weakness ahead of Fed cuts. The 30-year is the clearest signal of inflation expectations and currency sustainability. A 30-year yield at 2007 highs while the Fed is about to cut rates is the market saying: 'Rate cuts are coming, but they will weaken the dollar, push oil higher, and force yields to rise further before stabilizing.' This is the script that played out in 1979–80 (second oil shock) and early 2022 (inflation surprise followed by policy reversal).

open_watchlist.condition: Oil closes above $95 for three consecutive trading days
open_watchlist.meaning: Ceasefire framework is breaking; inflation expectations reset higher and the Fed's rate-cut narrative becomes untenable.

open_watchlist.condition: Fed official (Powell, regional president, or board member) makes public statement on rate cuts referencing external supply shocks rather than domestic labor market weakness
open_watchlist.meaning: The Fed is explicitly abandoning the independence narrative and pivoting to a supply-shock justification for cuts—a legal cover for political accommodation.

open_watchlist.condition: April consumer spending data (May 29 release) shows MoM change of 0% or negative
open_watchlist.meaning: Confirms that credit tightening is already hitting household purchasing power, justifying Fed cuts and triggering a bear-case scenario of inflation + weakening demand.

open_watchlist.condition: Third major lender (Discover, Capital One, American Express) cuts deposit rates or tightens credit within 7 days
open_watchlist.meaning: Accelerates the institutional signal that credit contraction is coordinated, not random, and creates a feedback loop where lenders frontrun Fed cuts and consumers lose purchasing power before unemployment rises.

open_watchlist.condition: Dollar index (DXY) closes below 100 for five consecutive trading days
open_watchlist.meaning: Signals market pricing of Warsh-era rate cuts and oil persistence simultaneously; typically precedes a 12-18 month period of dollar weakness and imported inflation.

open_watchlist.condition: Oil closes above $95 for three consecutive trading days (any cause: Iran escalation, inventory data, Warsh hawkish signal, or geopolitical escalation)
open_watchlist.meaning: Warsh's first rate-cut decision becomes a test of whether he is data-dependent (hold on oil risk) or politically driven (cut anyway); a break confirms structural inflation is the binding constraint.

open_watchlist.condition: Third major lender (Discover, Capital One, American Express) cuts deposit rates or tightens consumer credit within 7 days
open_watchlist.meaning: Confirms credit contraction is not a two-lender anomaly but a systemic dynamic; validates that institutions are front-running Fed rate cuts by restricting credit now.

open_watchlist.condition: 30-year Treasury yield closes above 4.6% for two consecutive trading days
open_watchlist.meaning: Bond markets are explicitly rejecting the idea that Warsh's rate cuts will lower long-term yields; this signals preparation for a capitulation selloff in equities once consumer data arrives.

open_watchlist.condition: April consumer spending (released May 29) shows MoM change of 0% or negative
open_watchlist.meaning: Lenders' credit withdrawal is prophetic; demand is already softening despite job gains in May; Warsh must choose between cutting into weakness (capitulation scenario) or pausing to protect the dollar.

open_watchlist.condition: Warsh's first public statement as Fed chair does not explicitly reference oil or supply constraints as a reason for gradualism
open_watchlist.meaning: Warsh is either ignoring the constraint or confident it will self-resolve; if he ignores it, bond markets will extract a yield premium immediately, forcing a sharp correction in equities within 1–2 weeks.
